question.prompt: Nine athletes, no two of whom are the same height, try out for the basketball team. One at a time, they draw a wristband at random, without replacement, from a bag containing \(3\) blue bands, \(3\) red bands, and \(3\) green bands. They are divided into a blue group, a red group, and a green group. The tallest member of each group is named the group captain. What is the probability that the group captains are the three tallest athletes?

solutions.title: Follow the three tallest
solutions.explanation:
The three tallest athletes will all be captains exactly when their wristbands have three different colors. Sharing a color would prevent the shorter of two athletes from being captain. With different colors, each of the three is taller than every other athlete in their group.

The random draws distribute the nine individual bands uniformly among the athletes. Consequently, we can calculate as though the three tallest athletes draw first: rearranging the drawing order does not change the distribution of assignments.

The tallest athlete can receive any color. Among the eight remaining bands, six have a different color, so the probability that the second tallest receives a different color is \(6/8\).

If those first two colors differ, all three bands of the unused color remain among the seven remaining bands. The third tallest therefore receives that color with conditional probability \(3/7\).

Multiplying the successive probabilities gives
\[
\frac{6}{8}\cdot\frac{3}{7}=\boxed{\frac{9}{28}}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).

solutions.title: Count sets of three bands
solutions.explanation:
Only the set of bands received by the three tallest athletes matters, so we can count unordered selections of three bands.

Temporarily give each wristband a distinct label. Every three-band set is equally likely to reach these athletes: each set can be assigned to them in the same number of orders, and the remaining bands can be assigned to the other athletes in the same number of ways.

The number of possible sets is
\[
\binom{9}{3}=\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7}{3\cdot2\cdot1}=84.
\]
The denominator removes the six orders in which any particular set could be listed.

For all three athletes to be captains, their colors must be different. Otherwise, two of them share a group and the shorter cannot be captain. Conversely, three different colors make each athlete the tallest in their group.

A favorable set therefore contains one band of each color. Choosing one of the three blue bands, one of the three red bands, and one of the three green bands gives
\[
3\cdot3\cdot3=27
\]
favorable sets. Each is counted once because its colors distinguish the three selections.

Thus the probability is
\[
\frac{27}{84}=\boxed{\frac{9}{28}},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
